name: Florence
subtitle: Florentia to the Grand Duchy
description: Florence from the Roman colony on the Arno to the grand dukes of Tuscany: the Roman square under the medieval centre, the city of the guilds and towers, Brunelleschi's dome and the Medici city, the Uffizi, the Pitti and the Boboli, inside the walls of 1284–1333 on both banks with San Miniato on its hill. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Arno
water.blurb: The Arnus of the Romans, a mountain river that is a trickle in August and a torrent in November. Its water washed and dyed the wool that made Florence rich; its weirs (pescaie) turned the mills and fulling stocks; its floods of 1177, 1333 and 1557 swept away the bridges.

water.name: Mugnone
water.blurb: The torrent from Fiesole; in Roman times, on the usual reconstruction, it ran close under the west side of the colony to the Arno, roughly where Via de' Tornabuoni runs now.

water.name: Mugnone
water.blurb: Diverted round the city in the Middle Ages, the Mugnone ran outside the north-west walls, filling their ditch, and joined the Arno below the Prato. It was moved again for the Fortezza da Basso in the 1530s.

hills.name: Boboli hill
hills.blurb: The hill behind the Pitti, quarried for the palace's stone. Cosimo I and Eleonora of Toledo bought it in 1549 and Tribolo, Ammannati and Buontalenti laid out the Boboli Gardens on its slope.

hills.name: Monte alle Croci
hills.blurb: The hill of San Miniato, south-east of the city across the river, with the abbey church on its crest. Michelangelo fortified it with earth bastions during the siege of 1529–30.

hills.name: Bellosguardo
hills.blurb: A hill of villas south-west of the walls, named for its view over the city.

roads.name: Cardo maximus (Via Roma, Via Calimala)
roads.blurb: The main north–south street of the colony, from the north gate past the forum to the south gate and the river; Via Roma, Via Calimala and Via Por Santa Maria still follow it.

roads.name: Decumanus maximus (Via Strozzi, Via del Corso)
roads.blurb: The east–west street through the forum, between the west and east gates; Via degli Strozzi, Via degli Speziali and Via del Corso keep its line.

roads.name: Via Cassia (to Rome)
roads.blurb: The consular road from Rome, which crossed the Arno here; the reason the colony was put on this spot.

roads.name: Road to Faesulae
roads.blurb: North-east to the old Etruscan hill town of Faesulae (Fiesole), and on over the Apennines toward Bononia.

roads.name: Road to Pisa
roads.blurb: West along the river toward Pistoria and Pisa.

roads.name: Via Calimala and Por Santa Maria
roads.blurb: The old cardo, the spine of the merchants' city: the cloth-finishers of the Calimala guild, the bankers at the Mercato Nuovo, the silk guild at Por Santa Maria, and the Ponte Vecchio at the end.

roads.name: Via de' Calzaiuoli
roads.blurb: The street of the hosiers between the cathedral and the Piazza della Signoria, past Orsanmichele: the processional way between church and state, widened in the 1380s.

roads.name: Via del Corso and Borgo degli Albizi
roads.blurb: The Roman decumanus continued east toward San Pier Maggiore, lined with the houses of the Albizi.

roads.name: Via de' Tornabuoni
roads.blurb: From the Ponte Santa Trinita north toward Santa Maria Novella, along the line of the Roman west wall; the street of the Strozzi, Rucellai and Tornabuoni palaces.

roads.name: Via Larga
roads.blurb: The 'wide street' north from the cathedral past the Medici palace and San Marco toward the Porta San Gallo; the Medici built their palace on it in the 1440s. Today Via Cavour.

roads.name: Via de' Servi
roads.blurb: From the cathedral to the church of the Servites at the Santissima Annunziata, lined with the palaces of their patrons.

roads.name: Borgo la Croce
roads.blurb: East through Sant'Ambrogio to the Porta alla Croce and the road to Arezzo; condemned men were led out further south, along the Via de' Malcontenti, to the gallows at the Porta alla Giustizia.

roads.name: Via de' Benci
roads.blurb: From Santa Croce down to the Ponte alle Grazie, past the palaces of the Alberti.

roads.name: Borgo Ognissanti and Via il Prato
roads.blurb: West past the Umiliati's wool workshops at Ognissanti to the Prato, the meadow inside the gate where races and fairs were held.

roads.name: Via Guicciardini
roads.blurb: From the Ponte Vecchio past Santa Felicita to the Piazza de' Pitti.

roads.name: Via Maggio and Via Romana
roads.blurb: Via Maggio, the 'greater street' of the Oltrarno, from the Ponte Santa Trinita south, continued by Via Romana to the Porta Romana and the road to Siena and Rome.

roads.name: Borgo San Frediano
roads.blurb: The street of the poorest wool workers, the dyers' and weavers' quarter of the Oltrarno, out to the Porta San Frediano and the road to Pisa.

roads.name: Via de' Bardi and Via San Niccolò
roads.blurb: Along the left bank under the hill, past the towers of the Bardi, the bankers ruined in the 1340s.

roads.name: Via del Monte alle Croci
roads.blurb: The steep path up to San Miniato, lined with the stations of the cross that gave the hill its name.

walls.name: Wall of Florentia
walls.blurb: The colony's wall, roughly 1.8 km round, with round towers and a gate on each side; traces turn up under the streets that follow its line, Via de' Tornabuoni on the west and Via del Proconsolo on the east.

walls.name: Walls of 1172 (right bank)
walls.blurb: The second circuit of the commune, built 1172–75, roughly on the usual reconstruction: it took in the suburbs round San Lorenzo and the cathedral but left the friars' new churches outside. By 1300 the city had spilled far beyond it and a third circuit was being built.

walls.name: Walls of 1172 (Oltrarno)
walls.blurb: The first wall round the Oltrarno, built with the 1172 circuit and approximate here: it enclosed the bridgeheads, Borgo San Jacopo and the streets round Santo Spirito.

walls.name: Walls of 1284–1333 (right bank)
walls.blurb: The third and last circuit, begun in 1284 and finished in 1333: 8.5 km in all, about 11.6 m high, a tower every 115 m or so and a moat. It enclosed so much land that the city did not fill it before the 19th century.

walls.name: Walls of 1284–1333 (Oltrarno)
walls.blurb: The left-bank half of the last walls, climbing from the river at San Frediano over the hills to San Niccolò. Michelangelo strengthened the hill stretch with earthworks in 1529; Forte Belvedere was built into it in the 1590s.

bridges.name: Roman bridge
bridges.blurb: The bridge of the Via Cassia, probably on stone piers with a timber deck, a little upstream of the later Ponte Vecchio on the line of the cardo; its exact position is a reconstruction.

bridges.name: Ponte Vecchio
bridges.blurb: The 'old bridge', for centuries the only one.

bridges.name: Ponte Santa Trinita
bridges.blurb: The bridge from Via de' Tornabuoni to Via Maggio.

bridges.name: Ponte alla Carraia
bridges.blurb: Built 1218–20 as the Ponte Nuovo, the second bridge of the city, for the carts (carri) of the wool trade. In 1304 it collapsed under a crowd watching a play of Hell staged on boats; rebuilt after the floods of 1333 and 1557, the second time by Ammannati.

blocks.name: Suburb of the theatre and amphitheatre
San Lorenzo and the cathedral quarter
San Pier Maggiore and the Corso
Santa Trinita and Por Santa Maria
San Piero Scheraggio and the Bargello
Borgo San Lorenzo and San Gallo
Borgo Pinti and Borgo la Croce
Santa Maria Novella and San Lorenzo
Santa Trinita and the Mercato Nuovo
Via Romana and San Pier Gattolino
Via della Scala and the Prato

districts.name: Colonia Florentia
districts.description: The walled colony: four quarters of a regular grid round the forum, the houses of veterans and traders, shops under the porticoes of the cardo.

districts.name: Oltrarno
districts.description: The sesto across the river, walled in 1173: the Bardi and Frescobaldi bankers along the bank, the Augustinians at Santo Spirito, dyers and weavers toward San Frediano.

districts.name: Quartiere di Santo Spirito
districts.description: The Oltrarno, one of the four quarters into which the city was divided from 1343: palaces of old families along Via Maggio, the Pitti, and the workers' streets of San Frediano.

districts.name: Quartiere di Santa Croce
districts.description: The south-east quarter, from the Piazza della Signoria to the Franciscans: the dyers and wool-workers of the Corso dei Tintori, the Bargello and the Stinche prison.

districts.name: Quartiere di San Giovanni
districts.description: The quarter of the Baptistery: the cathedral, San Lorenzo and the Medici palace on Via Larga, San Marco and the Annunziata with the Innocenti.

districts.name: Quartiere di Santa Maria Novella
districts.description: The north-west quarter: the Dominicans, the Rucellai and Strozzi palaces, the Umiliati at Ognissanti and the meadow of the Prato.

periods.label: Roman Florentia
periods.summary: Florentia, a colony of veterans on the north bank of the Arno where the Via Cassia crossed the river: a walled square about 500 by 420 m on a regular grid, the forum and Capitolium at the crossing of cardo and decumanus, baths, a theatre and, outside the walls to the east, an amphitheatre. Brick, local sandstone, plaster and red tile.
periods.feel: Carts rumbling over the timber bridge, smoke from the bath furnaces, fullers treading cloth in tubs by the river.

houses.title: Houses of Florentia
houses.text: Insulae of the gridded colony: brick and rubble houses round small courts and shops opening on the porticoed streets, plastered and roofed with red tile; richer domus with mosaics and gardens near the forum.

outskirts.title: Centuriated fields
outskirts.text: The plain was divided into square fields by the Roman survey; farmhouses, vineyards and potters' kilns along the roads to Faesulae, Pisa and Rome, tombs lining the roads out of the gates.

periods.label: Dante's Florence
periods.summary: The commune at its height: a banking and wool city of about 100,000 under the priors of the guilds, still bristling with the stone towers of the magnate families. The new cathedral rises round old Santa Reparata, the Palazzo dei Priori is being built, the friars build Santa Croce and Santa Maria Novella, and a third, far larger circuit of walls is going up.
periods.feel: Bells of a hundred churches, the clatter of looms and fulling mills, Guelf and Ghibelline shouting in the narrow streets under the towers.

houses.title: Case-torri and botteghe
houses.text: Narrow houses of stone and plaster three or four storeys high over open shops (botteghe) with wooden shutters, crowded round the stone towers of the great families, cut down to 29 m by the commune in 1250; wooden balconies and sporti jut over the lanes.

outskirts.title: Borghi and orti
outskirts.text: Ribbon suburbs (borghi) along the roads out of the gates, the friars' new convents, and wide orchards and vegetable gardens (orti) inside the line of the new walls.

periods.label: The Medici city
periods.summary: Florence under Lorenzo the Magnificent, unofficial ruler of a republic: Brunelleschi's dome (closed 1436) over the city, the new palaces of the bankers with rusticated stone fronts, the Innocenti, San Lorenzo and Santo Spirito in the new style, the workshops of painters and sculptors. The city fills only part of its walls, with gardens between the convents.
periods.feel: Hammering from the marble yards, the smell of dye vats and wool grease along the river, friars preaching to crowds in the piazzas.

houses.title: Botteghe and palazzi
houses.text: Rows of plastered houses over shops, now joined by the bankers' palazzi: a block of pietra forte with a rusticated ground floor, round-arched windows in pairs, a deep cornice, an arcaded courtyard and a bench along the street front.

outskirts.title: Convent gardens and orti
outskirts.text: Inside the walls, the gardens and orchards of the convents and the vegetable plots of the market gardeners; beyond, villas and farms on the hills, olive groves and vines.

periods.label: Grand-ducal Florence
periods.summary: The capital of the Medici grand dukes of Tuscany after the fall of the republic in 1530: the Fortezza da Basso over the city, the Uffizi offices and Vasari's corridor from the Palazzo Vecchio to the Pitti, the Boboli Gardens on the hill behind it, Forte Belvedere above them, new bridges by Ammannati. In October 1600 the Pitti saw the first surviving opera.
periods.feel: Court carriages on the new bridges, goldsmiths' hammers on the Ponte Vecchio, the bells of the convents and the snap of the grand duke's soldiers drilling in the fortress.

houses.title: Palazzi and case
houses.text: Plastered houses of three to five storeys over shops, the old towers cut down and built into them; the courtiers' new palazzi along Via Maggio and Via Tornabuoni with rusticated doorways, kneeling windows and coats of arms.

outskirts.title: Orti and Medici farms
outskirts.text: Orchards and kitchen gardens of the convents inside the walls; outside, the grand duke's dairy farm and meadows at the Cascine, villas and podere on the hills.

landmarks.name: Santa Maria del Fiore (the Duomo)

florentia-100.note: Roman houses with mosaic floors lay here just outside the north wall of the colony; the early Christian church of Santa Reparata was built over them, probably in the 5th–6th century.

comune-1300.name: Santa Reparata and the new cathedral
comune-1300.note: Old Santa Reparata, a Romanesque basilica, still serves as the cathedral. Arnolfo di Cambio's new church, founded on 8 September 1296, rises round it: the lower façade and the first bays of the new walls.

medici-1490.note: Brunelleschi's dome was closed in 1436 and its marble lantern finished in 1461; Verrocchio's gilt copper ball went up in 1471. The façade is still Arnolfo's half-finished front.

grand-ducal-1600.note: The cathedral of the grand dukes. Arnolfo's unfinished façade was pulled down in 1587; a painted temporary front was put up for Ferdinando I's wedding in 1589. Vasari and Zuccari frescoed the dome, 1572–79.

landmarks.summary: The cathedral of Florence, begun by Arnolfo di Cambio in 1296 and crowned by Filippo Brunelleschi's octagonal brick dome, 1420–36, still the largest masonry dome in the world, over a nave clad in white, green and pink marble.
details: Arnolfo's plan grew under Francesco Talenti and others into a vast nave of four bays ending in an octagon with three polygonal tribunes. Nobody knew how to vault the 45 m octagon until Brunelleschi built a double shell of brick in herringbone courses without centring, braced by stone and timber chains. The dome was closed in 1436; the lantern followed after his death in 1446.

The miniature shows the cathedral as it stood about 1490: the marble-banded nave with its pointed windows and side doors, the three tribunes with their half-domes and blind arcades, the drum with its oculi, the eight white ribs and red tiles of the dome, the lantern, and the unfinished façade. Giotto's campanile and the Baptistery are separate models.

landmarks.name: Baptistery of San Giovanni

florentia-100.note: A Roman building, probably a house with a bakery or a workshop, stood here just outside the colony's north gate; its pavements have been found under the Baptistery floor.

comune-1300.note: Every Florentine was baptised here, Dante among them ('il mio bel San Giovanni'). Andrea Pisano's bronze south doors will follow in 1330–36; the mosaics of the dome are being finished.

medici-1490.note: Ghiberti's two pairs of gilt bronze doors are in place: the north doors (1403–24) and the east 'Gates of Paradise' (1425–52), facing the cathedral.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Unchanged outside; Florentines still believed it was an ancient temple of Mars turned into a church.

landmarks.summary: An octagonal church of white and green marble in front of the cathedral, consecrated in 1059 and dedicated to Saint John, patron of Florence; Florentines believed it was a Roman temple of Mars.
details: The octagon, about 25.6 m across, is built of stone faced with white Carrara and green Prato marble in a geometric pattern of pilasters, arches and panels. A low pyramid roof hides the dome inside, covered with 13th-century mosaics of the Last Judgement; a lantern crowns it, and a rectangular apse, the scarsella, projects on the west.

The model shows the three storeys of the marble skin, the attic with its stripes, the white pyramid roof and lantern, the scarsella, and the three bronze-doored portals on the north, east and south as dark gilded panels. The columns of porphyry by the east door are left out.

landmarks.name: Giotto's Campanile

comune-1300.note: Not yet begun. Giotto, made master of the cathedral works in 1334, laid the first stone on 18 July of that year; Andrea Pisano and Francesco Talenti finished it in 1359.

medici-1490.note: Complete, 84.7 m, its lower storeys carved with hexagonal reliefs of the arts and trades by Andrea Pisano and Luca della Robbia.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Unchanged; the spire Giotto planned on top was never built.

landmarks.summary: The free-standing bell tower of the cathedral, 84.7 m high and 14.45 m square, faced in white, green and pink marble like the cathedral and designed by Giotto in 1334.
details: Giotto built only the lowest storey before he died in 1337. Andrea Pisano added the second, with niches for statues, and Francesco Talenti the three upper storeys with ever larger Gothic windows, closing the tower in 1359 with a projecting cornice instead of the planned spire.

The model has the square shaft with octagonal buttresses at the corners, the two relief zones, the statue niches, the paired and tripled windows of the upper storeys and the crowning cornice on corbels.

landmarks.name: Palazzo della Signoria (Palazzo Vecchio)

florentia-100.note: The Roman theatre of Florentia stood partly under the site, its curved seating facing north-east; its foundations survive beneath the palace.

comune-1300.name: Palazzo dei Priori (building)
comune-1300.note: Begun in 1299, probably to designs by Arnolfo di Cambio, on land of the Ghibelline Uberti, whose houses were razed. The priors moved in by 1302; the tower was finished about 1310.

medici-1490.note: The seat of the Signoria. The Medici rule from their own palace, but laws and elections pass here. The Great Council's hall follows in 1495, Michelangelo's David at the door in 1504.

grand-ducal-1600.name: Palazzo Vecchio
grand-ducal-1600.note: Cosimo I moved in in 1540; when the court went to the Pitti in the 1560s it became the 'old palace'. Vasari rebuilt the inside and the Uffizi and Corridor link it to the river.

landmarks.summary: The town hall of Florence: a fortress-like block of rough pietra forte with a projecting gallery of machicolations and crenellations, and a tower 94 m high set off-balance on its front.
details: Built from 1299 for the priors of the guilds, who lived shut inside it during their two-month terms. The block is rusticated stone with Guelf (square) battlements on the gallery and Ghibelline (swallow-tail) merlons on the tower, which rests on the gallery's corbels. The ringhiera, a platform for speakers, ran along the front onto the piazza.

The miniature shows the palace as it was about 1490: three storeys with paired Gothic windows, the gallery on corbels, the tower with its own machicolated gallery, belfry and bell cage, and the ringhiera. The later wings to the east, added from 1495 to 1600, are only hinted at.
landmarks.function: Seat of the priors and the Signoria, later the ducal palace

landmarks.name: Loggia della Signoria (Loggia dei Lanzi)

comune-1300.note: Not yet built: the corner of the piazza was still houses and the little church of San Romolo, and public ceremonies were held on the ringhiera of the palace.

medici-1490.note: An open hall for state ceremonies, swearing-in of officials and the reception of ambassadors, built 1376–82 by Benci di Cione and Simone Talenti. Donatello's Judith will be placed here in 1506.

grand-ducal-1600.name: Loggia dei Lanzi
grand-ducal-1600.note: Named after Cosimo I's German landsknecht guards (lanzi) quartered here. Cellini's Perseus (1554) and Giambologna's Rape of the Sabines (1583) stand under its arches.

landmarks.summary: A broad, open loggia of three round arches on clustered piers facing the Piazza della Signoria, built for the ceremonies of the republic and later turned into an open-air sculpture gallery.
details: Three wide arches face the piazza and one opens at each end. The arches are round, a classical touch in a Gothic building, with quatrefoils of the Virtues by Agnolo Gaddi's circle in the spandrels and a crenellated terrace on top from which the Medici watched festivals.

The model shows the deep vaulted hall behind the arches, the clustered piers, the four Virtues as roundels and the parapet. In the 1600 version Cellini's Perseus and Giambologna's group stand at the front arches.

landmarks.name: Uffizi

medici-1490.note: The site was a tangle of houses, the old mint (Zecca) and the Romanesque church of San Piero Scheraggio, where the councils of the commune had once met.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Begun in 1560 by Vasari for the offices (uffizi) of the thirteen magistracies; finished by Buontalenti and Alfonso Parigi in 1581. Francesco I opened the top-floor gallery and the octagonal Tribuna for his collections.

landmarks.summary: Vasari's long U-shaped office building of 1560–81, running from the Piazza della Signoria down to the Arno, its two long arcaded wings joined at the river by an open serliana.
details: Cosimo I wanted all the city's magistracies under one roof close to his palace. Vasari built two long wings of identical bays in grey pietra serena and white plaster on a Doric portico, closed toward the river by a short wing pierced by a great arch. The top floor became the Medici gallery; the corridor to the Pitti starts here.

The model shows the two long wings with their portico, three storeys of windows, the open loggia of the top floor and the river wing with its arch. The Tribuna and the Medici Theatre inside are not shown.
landmarks.function: Offices of the grand-ducal magistracies; the Medici gallery

landmarks.name: Ponte Vecchio

florentia-100.note: The Roman bridge of the Via Cassia crossed a little upstream, on the line of the cardo.

comune-1300.name: Ponte Vecchio (the old bridge)
comune-1300.note: The bridge rebuilt in stone in the 12th century after a flood, with timber shops; a statue said to be of Mars stood at its north end, where Buondelmonte was murdered in 1216. Lost in 1333.

medici-1490.note: Rebuilt in 1345, probably by Neri di Fioravanti, on three flat segmental arches, with shops of butchers and tanners, who threw their waste into the river.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Vasari's corridor of 1565 runs over the eastern shops. In 1593 Ferdinando I expelled the butchers and gave the shops to goldsmiths; back rooms (retrobotteghe) hang over the water on brackets.

landmarks.summary: The 'old bridge', for centuries the only one at the city's narrowest crossing: three stone arches of 1345 carrying two rows of shops, with an open terrace in the middle.
details: The 1345 bridge was among the first in Europe with segmental arches, lower and flatter than half-circles, which let it ride out floods that took the others. The commune let the shops to butchers, fishmongers and tanners; the middle was left open as a piazza with a view of the river.

The model shows the three arches on their cutwater piers, two rows of shops of uneven heights with back rooms hanging on timber brackets, and the open middle. The 1600 version adds Vasari's corridor along the east side with its round windows.

landmarks.name: Ponte alle Grazie

comune-1300.name: Ponte Rubaconte
comune-1300.note: Built in 1237 under the podestà Rubaconte da Mandello, the longest bridge of the city; it will survive the flood of 1333 that takes the others.

medici-1490.name: Ponte alle Grazie
medici-1490.note: Named after a shrine of the Madonna delle Grazie on one pier. Little houses and chapels stand on its piers, some of them cells of hermit women, the 'Murate', walled in for life.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Still standing on its nine arches with the little buildings on its piers, the bridge the floods of 1333 and 1557 could not take. (Blown up by the Germans in 1944.)

landmarks.summary: The upstream bridge, built in 1237 on nine stone arches, with small chapels, shops and hermits' cells on its piers; it was the one bridge the great floods never carried away.
details: Built to serve the growing suburbs round Santa Croce and San Niccolò, it was long called after the podestà who built it. Later houses and oratories were raised on its broad piers; the Madonna delle Grazie in one of them gave the bridge its later name. It stood until 1944.
The model shows the nine low arches on cutwater piers, the narrow roadway and the little buildings on the piers. The number and form of the houses are simplified from views of the 16th–17th century.

landmarks.name: Ponte Santa Trinita

comune-1300.note: First built of wood in 1252 by the Frescobaldi, rebuilt in stone after the flood of 1259 and swept away again in 1333.

medici-1490.note: The stone bridge rebuilt after 1333 (finished 1346), on five or six round arches; the flood of 1557 will destroy it.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Ammannati's bridge of 1567–69, perhaps on Michelangelo's advice: three flat elliptical arches of stone, the most elegant bridge of the Renaissance. Statues of the Seasons were added for the 1608 wedding.

landmarks.summary: The bridge from Via de' Tornabuoni to Via Maggio. Ammannati's bridge of 1569 spans the Arno in three shallow elliptical arches, so flat they seem to float.
details: After the flood of 1557 Cosimo I commissioned Bartolomeo Ammannati, who used arches of a curve still argued over (catenary or elliptical), with sharp cutwater piers and cartouches with the Medici arms at the crowns. Destroyed in 1944, it was rebuilt from the original stones dredged from the river.

The 1600 model shows the three flat arches, the pointed piers, the parapets and the crown cartouches. The earlier bridges are drawn as generic medieval bridges on round arches, since their form is little known.

landmarks.name: Palazzo del Bargello

comune-1300.name: Palazzo del Podestà
comune-1300.note: The first public palace of the commune, begun in 1255 for the Capitano del Popolo, then seat of the podestà, the foreign magistrate who judged. Dante was condemned in his court in 1302.

medici-1490.name: Palazzo del Podestà
medici-1490.note: The court of the podestà. After the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478 Botticelli painted the hanged conspirators in effigy on its walls, as the custom was for traitors.

grand-ducal-1600.name: Bargello
grand-ducal-1600.note: From 1574 the seat of the bargello, the chief of police, with its prison and torture chamber; executions took place in the courtyard.

landmarks.summary: The oldest public palace of Florence, begun in 1255: a stern block of pietra forte with crenellations and a tower, around a courtyard with an open staircase.
details: Built for the Capitano del Popolo after the popular rising of 1250 and enlarged in the 14th century, it incorporates the older Volognana tower, 57 m high. The courtyard with its outside staircase and loggia is hung with the stone coats of arms of the podestà.

The model shows the rusticated block with its few windows, Guelf crenellations on corbels, the tower with its own crenellated top, and the inner courtyard with the stair. The extension to the east is merged into one block.
landmarks.function: Seat of the podestà; later police headquarters and prison

landmarks.name: Orsanmichele

comune-1300.name: Loggia of the grain market
comune-1300.note: An open grain loggia of 1290, perhaps by Arnolfo, on the site of the garden-church of San Michele; a miracle-working image of the Madonna on one pier drew crowds of pilgrims. It burned in 1304.

medici-1490.note: Rebuilt from 1337 as grain market and granary; the arches were walled up about 1380 to make a church. The guilds set their patron saints in its niches: Donatello's Saint George, Ghiberti's Baptist.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Unchanged outside. In 1569 Cosimo I turned the upper floors into the archive of notarial contracts; chutes in the piers recall the old granary.

landmarks.summary: A tall square block of stone, granary above and church below, ringed with fourteen niches where the guilds set statues of their patron saints by Ghiberti, Donatello and Verrocchio.
details: The grain market of 1337 had open arcades below two storeys of granaries. After the arches were closed with Gothic tracery the ground floor became a church with Orcagna's marble tabernacle. Each guild had a niche on the outside to fill with its saint; the competition between them produced some of the first great Renaissance statues.
The model shows the three-storey block, the tracery of the closed arcades, the niches with statues, the upper windows and the cornice. The bridge to the Arte della Lana's palace is left out.
landmarks.function: Grain market and granary; church of the guilds

landmarks.name: Palazzo Medici

comune-1300.note: Houses and gardens on the Via Larga; the Medici, a family of moneychangers and wool merchants, still lived near the Mercato Vecchio.

medici-1490.note: Built for Cosimo the Elder from 1444 by Michelozzo; Lorenzo the Magnificent keeps his court, his antiquities and his circle of poets and scholars here. The corner is an open loggia.

grand-ducal-1600.note: The dukes moved out to the Palazzo Vecchio in 1540; the corner loggia was walled up in 1517 with Michelangelo's 'kneeling' windows. The Riccardi will buy it in 1659.

landmarks.summary: Michelozzo's palace for Cosimo de' Medici: the model of the Renaissance palazzo, its storeys growing smoother as they rise from rough rustication to smooth ashlar, under a huge classical cornice.
details: Cosimo is said to have rejected Brunelleschi's grander design as too likely to cause envy. Michelozzo built a cube round an arcaded courtyard with a garden behind: three storeys of stone, each less rusticated than the one below, arched windows in pairs, and a cornice projecting 2.5 m. Benozzo Gozzoli frescoed the chapel in 1459.

The miniature shows the palace before the Riccardi extended it: the three graded storeys, double windows, cornice, open corner loggia, courtyard and walled garden. The stone benches along the street are a thin band.

landmarks.name: San Lorenzo

florentia-100.note: Fields outside the colony on the road north; a church of San Lorenzo, consecrated by Saint Ambrose in 393, would be built here, the first cathedral of Florence.

comune-1300.name: San Lorenzo (Romanesque church)
comune-1300.note: The Romanesque basilica rebuilt about 1060, a collegiate church of canons with a bell tower, in the borgo north of the cathedral.

medici-1490.note: Brunelleschi's church, begun in 1421 with the Old Sacristy (finished 1428) paid for by Giovanni de' Medici, the nave finished after his death; the Medici parish and burial church. The façade is bare brick.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Michelangelo's New Sacristy (1520–34) and Laurentian Library (from 1524) have been added. His design for a marble façade was never built; the Chapel of the Princes is begun in 1604.

landmarks.summary: The Medici parish church, rebuilt by Brunelleschi from 1421: a basilica of grey pietra serena and white plaster with a low dome over the crossing, the Old Sacristy, and a façade still of rough brick.
details: Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici paid for the Old Sacristy, a cube under a ribbed umbrella dome, Brunelleschi's first completed building and the Medici tomb chapel. The nave, with its rows of Corinthian columns and side chapels, was built slowly after 1442 and finished about 1480.

The model shows the nave and aisles with chapels, the transept and crossing dome with lantern, the Old Sacristy with its small lantern on the north-west, and the rough brick front. Cloister and canons' buildings are left out.

landmarks.name: Santa Croce

florentia-100.note: Low, flood-prone ground by the river, east of the amphitheatre.

comune-1300.name: Santa Croce (building)
comune-1300.note: The Franciscans' small church of 1228 still stands while Arnolfo's huge new church, begun in 1294 or 1295, rises from the east end; it will take until 1385 to finish.

medici-1490.note: Complete and consecrated in 1443, its façade still bare stone. Brunelleschi's Pazzi Chapel (from 1442) stands in the cloister; tombs of the city's great men line the nave.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Vasari removed the choir screen in 1566. Michelangelo was buried here in 1564, carried secretly from Rome. The piazza in front is the ground of the calcio.

landmarks.summary: The great church of the Franciscans, begun in 1294: a wide T-shaped hall under an open timber roof, the largest Franciscan church in the world, with the Pazzi Chapel in its cloister.
details: Built for preaching to crowds, it has a nave and aisles separated by tall octagonal piers, a straight transept lined with chapels painted by Giotto and his followers for the Bardi and Peruzzi, and a polygonal apse. The marble façade dates only from 1863.

The model shows the long nave under its gable roof, the aisles, the transept with its row of chapels, the apse with tall windows, the bare front and the Pazzi Chapel to the south. The 19th-century campanile and façade are left out.

landmarks.name: Santa Maria Novella

comune-1300.name: Santa Maria Novella (building)
comune-1300.note: The Dominicans' new church, begun about 1279 on the site of the small church of Santa Maria delle Vigne; the choir and transept are built, the nave is going up from the east.

medici-1490.note: Finished. Leon Battista Alberti completed the marble façade for Giovanni Rucellai, 1456–70, fitting a classical temple front with great scrolls onto the Gothic lower storey. Ghirlandaio paints the choir, 1485–90.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Vasari remodelled the inside in the 1560s. In the piazza in front the chariot race of the Palio dei Cocchi is run each June round two obelisks set up in 1608.

landmarks.summary: The Dominican church of the city, built from about 1279, with a striped Gothic nave and Alberti's marble façade of 1470 joining its high nave to its aisles with two great scrolls.
details: The friars built a wide vaulted nave of pointed arches with banded ribs, a short transept and a square chapel at the east; the Romanesque-Gothic campanile, with its spire, stands at the corner of the cloister. Masaccio painted the Trinity in its aisle around 1427.

The model shows the nave and aisles with round windows, the transept, the choir chapels, the campanile with its spire, and Alberti's façade of white and green marble with its pediment and scrolls. The cloisters and convent are omitted.

landmarks.name: Santo Spirito

comune-1300.note: The Augustinian friars' first church of 1250 stood here, facing its piazza in the Oltrarno; it burned down in 1471.

medici-1490.note: Brunelleschi's last church, designed in 1434 and built after his death; nearly finished, with its crossing dome, and consecrated in 1481. The plain plastered front hides an interior ringed by 38 semicircular chapels.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Baccio d'Agnolo's bell tower (1503–17) now stands beside the apse. The front is still the plain plaster of the 1480s.

landmarks.summary: Brunelleschi's last church, in the Oltrarno: a Latin cross whose aisles run all the way round, lined with semicircular chapels, under a dome on a drum, behind a plain plastered front.
details: Brunelleschi wanted the church turned round to face the river and its outer wall to show the curves of its 40 chapels; the friars built it facing the piazza and with a straight outer wall. The crossing dome follows his model; the façade was finished only as plain plaster with curved gables.

The model shows the nave and aisles, the transept arms of equal plan, the dome on its drum with lantern, the chapel walls and the plain front with its scroll gable. The 1600 version adds the campanile.

landmarks.name: Ospedale degli Innocenti

comune-1300.note: Orchards of Cafaggio outside the walls of 1172, round the young church of the Servites, the Santissima Annunziata.

medici-1490.note: The silk guild's foundling hospital, opened in 1445. Brunelleschi's loggia of 1419–27, nine arches on slender columns, is the first Renaissance building; Andrea della Robbia's blue roundels of swaddled babies (1487) are new.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Unchanged outside. The piazza has become a square of matching loggias, with Giambologna's statue of Ferdinando I (1608) to come.

landmarks.summary: The foundling hospital of Florence, opened in 1445, with Brunelleschi's loggia of nine round arches on Corinthian columns of grey pietra serena, the first building of the Renaissance.
details: Commissioned by the Arte della Seta, the silk guild, it took in abandoned babies, left in a basin under the loggia. Brunelleschi designed the portico on a module, every bay a cube, with columns, arches and window pediments in grey stone against white plaster. Behind it lie the cloisters of the men and women.
The model shows the raised loggia with its steps, the nine arches, the della Robbia roundels, the upper floor with its small pedimented windows, the church, and the two cloisters behind.

landmarks.name: Palazzo Pitti

comune-1300.note: Vineyards and quarries on the hill of Boboli above the Oltrarno; the stone of Florence's palaces came from here.

medici-1490.note: Begun about 1458 for the banker Luca Pitti, a rival of the Medici, on a scale meant to outdo them; perhaps after a design by Brunelleschi. Pitti's fortunes fell and the seven-bay block stands unfinished.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Bought by Eleonora of Toledo in 1549 and made the grand-ducal palace. Ammannati built the great rusticated courtyard (1560–77); the Boboli Gardens climb the hill behind. Euridice was sung here in 1600.

landmarks.summary: The palace of Luca Pitti, begun about 1458, a cliff of huge rough-hewn blocks with seven tall arched bays on each floor; from 1550 the palace of the Medici dukes, later grand dukes.
details: The original block had three storeys of seven bays in massive rustication. Under Cosimo I Ammannati added the courtyard behind, its three orders of rusticated columns opening onto the Boboli. The façade was stretched to thirteen bays in the 1620s and given its long wings later.

The 1490 model shows Pitti's seven-bay block with its rough rustication, terraces and central door. The 1600 model adds Ammannati's courtyard and wings, the grotto terrace and the start of the Boboli amphitheatre behind.
landmarks.function: Palace of the Pitti; grand-ducal residence

landmarks.name: San Miniato al Monte

florentia-100.note: A hillside above the river. According to legend, Minias, an Armenian prince or soldier, was beheaded about 250 CE and walked up here carrying his head to the place of his tomb.

comune-1300.note: The Romanesque church begun in 1018 by Bishop Hildebrand, with its marble front; the bishops' summer palace stands beside it (1295). The Benedictines of Cluny hold it, the Olivetans from 1373.

medici-1490.note: Michelozzo's marble Chapel of the Crucifix (1448) stands in the nave; the old bell tower collapsed in 1499 and a new one is being built.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Michelangelo hung mattresses on the new bell tower to save it from the imperial guns in 1530 and ringed the hill with bastions, made a permanent fortress by Cosimo I in 1553.

landmarks.summary: A Romanesque church on the hill south-east of the city, begun in 1018 over the tomb of the martyr Minias, its façade inlaid with white and green marble in a geometric pattern.
details: The church has a nave and aisles with a raised choir over a crypt, under an open timber roof. Its marble front, of the 11th and 12th centuries, has five arches below and a pedimented upper storey with a small temple window and a mosaic; a bronze eagle of the Calimala guild, its patrons, stands on top.
The model shows the nave and aisles, the raised choir and apse, the inlaid façade, the bell tower of 1523 and the bishop's palace beside it. The fortifications round the hill are left out.

landmarks.name: Fortezza da Basso

medici-1490.note: Gardens and the Porta Faenza on the city walls, with the Mugnone in the ditch beyond.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Built in 1534–35 for Duke Alessandro de' Medici by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, aimed at the city as much as its enemies. Alessandro was murdered in 1537; Cosimo I kept his troops here.

landmarks.summary: A huge pentagonal fortress of brick with angled bastions, built in 1534–35 across the north-west walls by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger to hold the city for the Medici.
details: Five bastions faced with brick, with stone quoins and a lozenge pattern of rusticated stone on the main bastion toward the city, enclose barracks, magazines and parade ground. It swallowed the old Porta Faenza, whose tower became the core of the keep.
The model shows the pentagon with its arrow-headed bastions, the wet ditch, the keep at the gate and the barracks inside. Proportions are simplified.

landmarks.name: Forte di Belvedere

medici-1490.note: Vineyards and the walls of 1333 on the crest of the hill above the Boboli.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Built 1590–95 by Bernardo Buontalenti for Ferdinando I on the crest above the Boboli, a star fort guarding the Pitti, with a villa (palazzina) at its heart.

landmarks.summary: The star fort on the hill above the Boboli, built by Buontalenti for Ferdinando I in 1590–95, with the grand duke's palazzina rising from the middle of its bastions.
details: The fort follows the ridge in an elongated star of bastions faced with stone, reached from the Boboli by a private path. Inside stands a three-storey villa with a loggia on top; the Medici are said to have kept part of their treasure in its vaults.
The model shows the bastioned walls on the slope, the palazzina with its loggia, and the gate. Bastion outlines are simplified.

landmarks.name: Forum and Capitolium of Florentia

florentia-100.note: The heart of the colony where cardo and decumanus crossed: a paved square with porticoes and shops, the Capitolium of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on its north side, and a basilica.

comune-1300.note: The Mercato Vecchio, the old market, filled the Roman forum: stalls of butchers, fishmongers and greengrocers round a column, under the towers of the old families.

medici-1490.note: Still the Mercato Vecchio, with Donatello's statue of Abundance on its column (c. 1430).

grand-ducal-1600.note: Still the market. In 1571 Cosimo I walled the Jews into a ghetto on its north-west side. (The square was demolished in the 1880s for the Piazza della Repubblica.)

landmarks.summary: The forum of Roman Florentia, where the Piazza della Repubblica is now: a porticoed square at the crossing of the main streets, with the Capitolium temple on its north side.
details: Excavations of the 1890s found the podium of the Capitolium, of the 1st century CE, and parts of the forum paving, the porticoes and shops. The square was about 100 by 70 m; the Capitolium stood on a high podium facing south down the cardo.

The miniature reconstructs the forum with porticoes on three sides, the Capitolium with its triple cella and steps, a basilica on the south side and a column in the middle. Sizes follow the usual reconstruction; much is conjecture.
landmarks.function: Forum and chief temple of the colony

landmarks.name: Amphitheatre of Florentia

florentia-100.note: Built in the 2nd century outside the walls to the south-east, for gladiators and wild beasts; perhaps 15,000 seats.

comune-1300.note: The ring of houses called the parlascio (from parlagium, arena) has grown into its arches; the Peruzzi built their palaces on its ruins. Via Torta and Via Bentaccordi follow its curve.

medici-1490.note: Gone except for the curve of the streets and walls built into the houses of the Peruzzi.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Gone; the curved streets remain.

landmarks.summary: The Roman amphitheatre outside the south-east corner of the colony, its oval preserved to this day in the curving line of Via Torta, Via Bentaccordi and Piazza de' Peruzzi.
details: The arena, roughly 113 by 90 m outside (estimates vary), was built of stone and brick in the early 2nd century. Its arches survive inside the cellars of the houses round Piazza de' Peruzzi; medieval Florentines called the ruin the parlascio.
The model shows the oval with two storeys of arches, the seating and the sand of the arena. Its size and orientation follow the curve of the medieval streets; heights are reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Porta Romana

comune-1300.note: Not yet built: the road to Siena and Rome left the Oltrarno by the older gate of San Pier Gattolino. The new gate was raised in 1326–28 as the last walls were finished.

medici-1490.note: The gate of the road to Siena and Rome, a tall tower of pietra forte over a single arch, with a fresco of the Madonna in the lunette.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Unchanged: the gate of the road to Siena and Rome, by which travellers from the south entered the grand duke's city.

landmarks.summary: The great south gate of the Oltrarno, built in 1326–28 on the walls of 1284–1333: a tall square tower of stone over the road to Siena and Rome, with a stretch of wall on either side.
details: Like the other gates of the last circuit it was a tower about 30 m high; most were cut down in the 16th century to make them less of a target for artillery. The wooden doors and their iron fittings still hang in the arch.
The model shows the gate tower with its arch, its outer front with the Madonna lunette, the crenellated top and a section of the city wall on each side.

spots.name: Baths of Florentia
spots.summary: A public bath in the south-west quarter of the colony, remembered in the name of the Via delle Terme; another bath building has been excavated under the Piazza della Signoria.
details: Florentia's baths were fed by the aqueduct from the slopes of Monte Morello. Excavations under the Piazza della Signoria in the 1980s found a bath with hypocaust floors next to a dyeworks and fullers' vats, the start of the city's long trade in cloth. The Via delle Terme bath is known mostly from its name and finds.

vignettes.text: The furnace boy feeds oak logs into the praefurnium; steam ghosts out of the vents into the cold air coming off the Arno.
Veterans of the colony, shopkeepers from the cardo and a cloth-dealer from Pisa sit in the warm room arguing about the price of wool.
The attendant scrapes the last bather with a strigil by lamplight; outside, carts creak toward the bridge before the gates shut.

spots.name: Theatre of Florentia
spots.summary: The colony's theatre, just outside its south-east corner, whose foundations lie under the Palazzo Vecchio and Via de' Gondi.
details: Built in the 1st century CE, its semicircular seating faced north-east and may have held some 7,000–10,000 people; parts of its walls and the radiating vaults under the seats can be seen beneath the Palazzo Vecchio. Like the amphitheatre nearby, it lay outside the walls.

vignettes.text: A slave sweeps the orchestra and sets out cushions for the magistrates' seats before the games of the festival.
A mime with a painted mask makes the crowd howl; vendors climb the steps with baskets of chickpeas and cheap wine.
The awnings are rolled in, the last spectators drift toward the east gate, and the stage-hands drag scenery back under the vaults.

spots.name: Shrine of Isis
spots.summary: A temple of the Egyptian goddess Isis, found under the Piazza San Firenze, east of the colony: a sign of the traders and freedmen from the eastern Mediterranean who lived here.
details: Remains of a sanctuary of Isis came to light near Piazza San Firenze, outside the east gate. Her cult, popular with merchants and sailors, came up the Arno from Pisa and the coast. Its form here is unknown; the spot marks its likely place.

vignettes.text: Priests with shaven heads open the temple doors at dawn and sprinkle water from the Nile, or what they say is the Nile, on the steps.
A freedwoman from Alexandria brings a lamp shaped like a boat and asks the goddess for a safe voyage for her son.
The rattle of the sistrum and a hymn in Greek drift over the wall into the street of the dyers.

spots.name: Dyers and wool-washers of the Corso dei Tintori
spots.summary: Along the river east of the Ponte alle Grazie the dyers and the wool-washers of the Arte della Lana worked at vats and wash-places, using the water of the Arno.
details: Raw English and Spanish wool was washed in the river, combed and spun in the countryside, woven in the city and brought back to be dyed and finished. The dyers' street, the Corso dei Tintori, kept its name. The wool guild regulated every step; the wool workers, the ciompi, had no guild of their own and rose in revolt in 1378.

vignettes.text: Barefoot men stand knee-deep at the wash-place treading bundles of greasy fleece; the water runs grey downstream toward the bridges.
Steam from the woad vats; a dyer lifts a length of cloth that comes up green and turns blue in the air, and his arms are blue to the elbow.
Cloth hangs on poles along the bank to dry. A guild official checks the seals and colours before the merchants' men carry it off.

medici-1490.note: The wool trade is past its 14th-century peak but still employs thousands; silk is the growing luxury.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Wool is in decline; silk and banking for the court matter more. The dyers stay by the river.

spots.name: An apothecary's shop (speziale)
spots.summary: A shop of the guild of physicians and apothecaries by the Mercato Vecchio: spices, drugs, wax, paper and painters' colours. Dante enrolled in this guild about 1295 so he could hold office.
details: The Arte dei Medici e Speziali was one of the seven major guilds. It took in doctors, apothecaries, grocers of spices, and painters, who bought their pigments from the speziali. After the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 only guild members could sit in government, so nobles and men of letters like Dante joined one.

vignettes.text: The apprentice takes down the shutters and lays out jars of pepper, ginger and saffron on the counter; a painter's boy waits for ultramarine.
A physician in a red gown dictates a remedy of rhubarb and honey while the speziale pounds it in a bronze mortar.
Candles of the shop's own wax burn while the master enters the day's sales in his book, in the merchant's careful hand.

spots.name: Houses of the Alighieri
spots.summary: The Alighieri, a family of small nobility, had houses in the parish of San Martino del Vescovo near the Badia, where Dante was born in 1265.
details: Dante grew up here among the houses of the Cerchi and the Donati, the families whose feud split the Guelfs into Whites and Blacks. By tradition he married Gemma Donati in the little church of San Martino. The 'Casa di Dante' shown today was rebuilt in 1910 near the old site.

vignettes.text: The bell of the Badia, which Dante remembered in Paradiso, rings terce across the lane; a servant goes out for bread and water.
Men of the Cerchi ride past armed, and the shutters of the Donati houses opposite slam. Nobody walks this street alone after the May Day brawl.
A lamp burns in an upper room. Dante is writing, perhaps the sonnets of the New Life, perhaps a letter for the priors.

spots.name: Mercato Vecchio
spots.summary: The old market on the site of the Roman forum: butchers, fishmongers, poulterers and greengrocers under the towers, with the column of Abundance in the middle.
details: The market filled the old forum and the lanes round it, with loggias of the butchers and fishmongers and the little churches of the old city. Sacchetti and other storytellers set their tricks and quarrels here. Donatello's statue of Abundance stood on a granite column from about 1430.

vignettes.text: Carts from the contado come in at the gates with cabbages, chestnuts and cheeses; the butchers hang out quarters of veal on iron hooks.
A housewife haggles over a pair of thrushes; a juggler, a quack selling theriac and a blind singer all compete for the crowd round the column.
The stalls come down; dogs fight over scraps and the sweepers sluice the paving with water from the well.

grand-ducal-1600.note: Still the market; from 1571 the Jewish ghetto, closed by gates at night, lies on its north-west side.

spots.name: Bankers' tables of the Mercato Nuovo
spots.summary: The new market by Por Santa Maria, where the changers and bankers of the Arte del Cambio sat at tables covered with green cloth, with their account books and purses.
details: A banker's table (tavola) was a bench with a cloth, a ledger and a bag of coins; the word banco gave us 'bank'. Money changed hands by written order in the books. The Medici bank, founded by Giovanni di Bicci in 1397, had branches from London to Rome and was the richest in Europe under Cosimo; it collapsed in 1494.

vignettes.text: The banker spreads his green cloth and his book on the bench; a wool merchant needs florins changed into Venetian ducats for a shipment.
A clerk reads out a bill of exchange drawn on Bruges; the banker checks the merchant's mark and enters the sum in his book.
The day's coins are counted and weighed, bad florins nailed to the counter, and the book carried home under guard.

comune-1300.note: The changers of the Cambio guild already sit here; the Bardi and Peruzzi are the great banks.

medici-1490.note: The Medici, like other banking houses, keep their Florentine table in this quarter; Lorenzo neglects the bank, which is failing.

grand-ducal-1600.name: Loggia del Mercato Nuovo
grand-ducal-1600.note: Cosimo I built a covered loggia here in 1547–51 for the silk and gold merchants and the bankers.

spots.name: Ghiberti's foundry
spots.summary: The workshop where Lorenzo Ghiberti cast the bronze doors of the Baptistery, 1403–52, probably near the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, a training ground for a generation of artists.
details: Ghiberti won the competition of 1401 for the Baptistery's north doors against Brunelleschi. Each panel was modelled in wax, cast in bronze by the lost-wax method, chased and gilded. Donatello, Michelozzo, Uccello and many others worked in his shop. The east doors took 27 years; Michelangelo called them worthy to be the gates of paradise.

vignettes.text: The furnace has been burning all night; assistants in leather aprons stand by the clay mould buried in the casting pit.
Molten bronze runs glowing into the mould with a hiss and a smell of burnt wax; Ghiberti watches without a word.
An apprentice works a chisel over the rough casting of a panel, chasing the curls of Isaac's hair, while the master draws the next scene.

spots.name: Verrocchio's bottega
spots.summary: The workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, sculptor, painter and goldsmith, in Via dell'Agnolo near Sant'Ambrogio, where Leonardo da Vinci trained from about 1466 alongside Perugino and Lorenzo di Credi.
details: A Florentine bottega took any job: altarpieces, bronze statues, tombs, banners for jousts, painted chests, the gilt ball on the cathedral's lantern. Apprentices ground colours, prepared panels and painted parts of the master's works; Leonardo painted an angel in Verrocchio's Baptism of Christ. Verrocchio died in Venice in 1488 and Lorenzo di Credi took over the shop.

vignettes.text: The youngest boy grinds lapis on a porphyry slab while another boils rabbit-skin glue for the gesso; the master is already at his clay model.
A young man from Vinci, beautiful and left-handed, is drawing drapery cast in plaster-soaked cloth, the folds lit by the window.
Clients come at evening: a monk with a contract for an altarpiece, a Medici steward to see how the bronze David is coming on.

spots.name: A silk merchant's shop in Por Santa Maria
spots.summary: The shop of a setaiolo, a silk manufacturer of the Arte di Por Santa Maria, who gave out raw silk to be spun, dyed and woven at home and sold the velvets and brocades.
details: Silk grew into the city's luxury trade in the 15th century. The guild of Por Santa Maria, which also took in goldsmiths, had its hall here. Weaving was done on home looms, often by women in the Oltrarno; the gold-brocaded velvets with pomegranate patterns went to princes and churches across Europe.

vignettes.text: A woman from San Frediano brings a finished bolt of crimson velvet; the factor measures it, checks the pile and pays her by the braccio.
A Genoese buyer fingers a brocade woven with gold thread; the price would buy a farm in the Mugello.
Bales are sewn into waxed cloth for the mule train to Bologna, and the master locks the gold thread in an iron chest.

spots.name: The foundlings' basin
spots.summary: At the end of the Innocenti loggia a basin (pila) behind an iron grille received abandoned babies, left by night, often with a token or a note to identify them later.
details: The hospital opened in 1445; its first foundling was a girl named Agata Smeralda. Babies were left in the pila, later in a turning wheel (ruota, from 1660), and given to wet-nurses in the country, then raised in the hospital. Many died; mothers left half-medals or scraps of cloth so they could reclaim a child one day.

vignettes.text: A woman wrapped in a shawl hurries across the empty piazza, lays a bundle in the basin, rings the bell and is gone before the door opens.
Wet-nurses from the Mugello wait under the loggia to be given babies to take home, with a stipend and a register number.
The prior's clerk writes in the great book: a boy, about two days old, with half a medal of Saint John tied to his wrist.

spots.name: Calcio in Piazza Santa Croce
spots.summary: The wide piazza in front of Santa Croce, ground of preaching, jousts and above all the calcio, Florentine football: two teams of 27 young men in livery, fighting for the ball with hands and feet.
details: Calcio was played in winter in the city's squares, the Piazza Santa Croce above all, between teams from the quarters or young nobles; the ground was spread with sand and fenced. Its rules were written down by Giovanni de' Bardi in 1580. Friars also preached here to crowds too large for the church.

vignettes.text: Workmen spread sand over the paving and set up the wooden fence; the Franciscans watch from the steps with disapproval and curiosity.
The ball goes up, trumpets, and 54 young men in green and white crash together; a nobleman's son comes out with a bloody nose and goes back in.
The winners parade with a calf as their prize; the losers drink in the taverns of Borgo la Croce and swear revenge next year.

spots.name: Le Stinche
spots.summary: The city prison, a windowless walled block on Via Ghibellina built from 1299, named after the castle of Le Stinche whose rebel garrison were its first inmates in 1304.
details: Debtors, the insane and political prisoners were held here; prisoners paid for their own food, and the confraternity of the Neri and other charities brought bread and paid debts to free them. Machiavelli was briefly held and tortured here in 1513 after the return of the Medici.

vignettes.text: Hands reach through the grating of the door for the bread a lay brother hands in from a basket.
A wife pays the jailer two soldi to pass a pot of soup and a clean shirt to her husband, held for a debt to a cloth merchant.
The bell rings for the night; the gaoler counts heads by lantern and bars the inner door.

comune-1300.note: Being built from 1299 on land of the Uberti; it will be in use from 1304.

spots.name: A goldsmith on the Ponte Vecchio
spots.summary: In 1593 Ferdinando I threw the butchers off the Ponte Vecchio, for the stench under his corridor, and gave the shops to goldsmiths and jewellers.
details: The bridge's shops were let by the city; the butchers had been there since 1442. Ferdinando's decree of 1593 reserved them for goldsmiths, who still keep them. Cellini, who learned his trade in shops like these, worked in gold, silver and bronze; his bust stands in the middle of the bridge since 1901.

vignettes.text: The goldsmith unbolts the wooden shutters, which fold down to make a counter; a boy blows up the little forge with a bellows.
A courtier's wife chooses a pendant set with a pearl; overhead, footsteps on the corridor floor, perhaps the grand duke himself.
The shutters close one by one along the bridge; below, the river runs dark under the back rooms on their brackets.

medici-1490.name: Butchers' shops on the Ponte Vecchio
medici-1490.note: The commune put the butchers here in 1442 to keep their smell out of the city; offal went straight into the Arno.

spots.name: Spezieria of Santa Maria Novella
spots.summary: The Dominican friars' pharmacy, where from the 13th century they made remedies, rosewater and distilled waters from their garden's herbs; it opened to the public in 1612.
details: The friars grew simples in their gardens and distilled waters, salves and elixirs for their infirmary. Under the grand dukes their spezieria became famous for its products, such as the 'acqua della regina' said to have been made for Catherine de' Medici; in 1612 it opened as a public shop.

vignettes.text: A lay brother in the garden cuts roses and lavender still wet with dew and carries them in to the stills.
Copper alembics drip into glass flasks; the friar writes labels in Latin and seals each stopper with wax.
A court lady's servant waits for a flask of rosewater and a pot of salve for chilblains; the bell rings for Vespers.

spots.name: A tavern off the Mercato Vecchio
spots.summary: A wine shop in the lanes round the old market, where wine was sold by the flask and gamblers played dice despite the laws against it.
details: Florentine taverns sold the city's red wine from the hills, bread, tripe and cheese. The commune taxed every barrel and banned dice games, often in vain. Sacchetti's stories are full of tavern tricks; the painters Buffalmacco and Bruno drank and plotted in such places in Boccaccio's tales.

vignettes.text: The taverner rinses his flasks at the well; the first customers are porters from the market, wanting bread and a glass.
Two painters argue about a client who will not pay; a wool-carder loses his week's wage at dice in the back room.
The night watch passes; the shutters are half-closed but singing comes from inside, and someone is sick in the lane.

events.title: Colonia Florentia founded
events.text: Veterans were settled on the Arno where the Via Cassia crossed it, perhaps under Caesar's land law of 59 BCE, perhaps under the triumvirs about 30 BCE. Surveyors laid out the walled square and the grid of the fields around. The name, 'flourishing', may come from the spring festival of Flora, when the colony was founded.

events.title: First stone of the new cathedral
events.text: On the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin the papal legate, Cardinal Pietro Valeriani, laid the first stone of the new cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, designed by Arnolfo di Cambio to be the largest church in Christendom, around the old Santa Reparata, which went on being used.

events.title: Dante condemned and exiled
events.text: After the Black Guelfs seized power with the help of Charles of Valois, the podestà Cante de' Gabrielli condemned Dante, away on an embassy to Rome, for corruption in office. In March the sentence became death by burning if he returned. He never did; he wrote the Divine Comedy in exile and died at Ravenna in 1321.

events.title: The great flood
events.text: After four days of rain the Arno rose over the city, water standing metres deep in the Piazza della Signoria and the Duomo. It swept away the Ponte Vecchio, the Ponte Santa Trinita and the Ponte alla Carraia; only the Rubaconte stood. Villani counted some 300 dead and blamed the city's sins.

events.title: The Black Death
events.text: The plague came in March and killed perhaps half the city by autumn; Giovanni Villani the chronicler died of it. Boccaccio described the mass graves and the abandoned sick, and set the meeting of his ten young storytellers of the Decameron one Tuesday morning in Santa Maria Novella, before they fled to the hills.

events.title: The cathedral consecrated under its dome
events.text: On the feast of the Annunciation, the Florentine new year, Pope Eugenius IV walked from his lodging at Santa Maria Novella to the cathedral along a raised wooden walkway hung with cloth, and consecrated it under Brunelleschi's newly closed dome. Dufay's motet Nuper rosarum flores was sung.

events.title: The Pazzi conspiracy
events.text: At High Mass in the cathedral the Pazzi and their allies, backed by the pope, struck at the Medici brothers. Giuliano died with nineteen wounds; Lorenzo, cut in the neck, escaped into the sacristy. The city rose for the Medici: Archbishop Salviati and Francesco de' Pazzi were hanged from the windows of the Palazzo della Signoria that evening.

events.title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
events.text: At Carnival the boys of Savonarola's bands, who had gone from house to house collecting, built a stepped pyramid in the Piazza della Signoria of mirrors, cosmetics, wigs, playing cards, lutes, books of Boccaccio and Petrarch and paintings, and set it alight while the crowd sang hymns.

events.title: Savonarola burned
events.text: Excommunicated, arrested after a failed ordeal by fire and tortured, the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola and two of his brothers were hanged and burned on a scaffold in the Piazza della Signoria, on the spot where the bonfire had been. Their ashes were thrown into the Arno from the Ponte Vecchio.

events.title: Michelangelo's David set up
events.text: The marble giant, carved from a block spoiled forty years before, was hauled from the cathedral workshop to the Piazza della Signoria in a wooden cage on greased beams, forty men at the winches, over four days in May. Stones were thrown at it by night. It was unveiled at the palace door on 8 September.

events.title: Calcio under siege
events.text: With the armies of the emperor and the pope camped on the hills round the city, the young men of the besieged republic played a game of calcio in Piazza Santa Croce, in livery, with musicians on the church roof, to show the enemy their contempt. The city surrendered in August and the Medici returned as dukes.

events.title: The Uffizi begun
events.text: Cosimo I had a whole quarter between his palace and the river cleared, the old church of San Piero Scheraggio cut down, and Giorgio Vasari began the long offices of the magistracies. The foundations on the soft river ground gave trouble; Vasari died in 1574 and Buontalenti finished the building.

events.title: The corridor in five months
events.text: For the wedding of Cosimo's son Francesco to Joanna of Austria in December 1565, Vasari built a covered passage about a kilometre long from the Palazzo Vecchio through the Uffizi, over the Ponte Vecchio and on to the Pitti, in about five months, so the duke could cross the city unseen. The Mannelli refused to let it through their tower, so it goes round.

events.title: The first surviving opera
events.text: Among the festivities for the proxy wedding of Maria de' Medici to Henry IV of France, Jacopo Peri's Euridice, on Ottavio Rinuccini's text, was sung in a room of the Pitti before a small court audience: a drama told entirely in music, the new style worked out by the Florentine Camerata. Peri sang Orpheus himself.

stories.title: Dante's city, 1300
stories.summary: Walk with Dante Alighieri, poet and guildsman, through the year he served as prior, when the city was at the height of its wealth and on the edge of the feud that would exile him.

steps.title: Among the Cerchi and the Donati
steps.text: Dante, 35, lives in his family's houses near the Badia, between the Cerchi, leaders of the White Guelfs, and the Donati of the Blacks, his wife's kin. On May Day young men of both families fight in the Piazza Santa Trinita.

steps.title: My beautiful San Giovanni
steps.text: Here he was baptised, like every Florentine; he once broke one of the marble fonts to save a boy who was drowning in it, he says in the Inferno. Mosaics of the Last Judgement shine in the dome.

steps.title: A guildsman
steps.text: To hold office a noble must belong to a guild. Dante joined the physicians and apothecaries about 1295; among the speziali's jars of pepper and pigment he is enrolled as 'Dante d'Aldighieri, poet'.

steps.title: The new cathedral rising
steps.text: Arnolfo's masons are building the new front around old Santa Reparata. The city means its cathedral to be the largest in the world; no one yet knows how its crossing will be roofed.

steps.title: Prior for two months
steps.text: As one of the six priors Dante votes to exile the leaders of both factions to calm the city, his friend the poet Guido Cavalcanti among them; Guido dies of fever that summer. Across the way the walls of the priors' new palace are rising.

steps.title: The stone at the bridge
steps.text: At the north end of the bridge stands the battered statue said to be of Mars. Here Buondelmonte was killed in 1216, the murder Florentines said began the war of Guelfs and Ghibellines.

steps.title: The sentence
steps.text: The Blacks are in power. In the podestà's court Dante, absent in Rome, is condemned for graft and banished; in March the sentence is death by fire. He will never see Florence again.

stories.title: An apprentice in the Medici city
stories.summary: Follow a boy apprenticed to Andrea del Verrocchio, as Leonardo was, through the workshop's commissions in the city of Lorenzo de' Medici in the 1470s.

steps.title: Grinding colours
steps.text: Your first year is spent grinding pigments, boiling glue and sweeping. You watch the older apprentices, one of them a notary's son from Vinci, draw drapery and paint angels into the master's pictures.

steps.title: Copying the doors
steps.text: On feast days the master sends you to draw from Ghiberti's gilded doors of the Baptistery, the school of every Florentine artist: perspective, figures, landscape, all in bronze.

steps.title: The ball on the lantern
steps.text: The shop has made the great copper ball for the top of Brunelleschi's lantern, gilded and soldered with burning-mirrors. Today it is hauled up with Brunelleschi's own hoists while the city watches and the bells ring.

steps.title: A tomb for the Medici
steps.text: In the Old Sacristy of San Lorenzo you help install the master's tomb for Piero and Giovanni de' Medici, Lorenzo's father and uncle: porphyry, marble and a net of bronze ropes.

steps.title: Christ and Saint Thomas
steps.text: For the merchants' court the master is casting a bronze Christ and doubting Thomas to fill a niche of Orsanmichele, Thomas half outside the niche as if stepping into the street.

steps.title: David goes to the Signoria
steps.text: The Medici sell the master's bronze David to the Signoria, and it is set up in the palace. You recognise in its face the young man from Vinci, who, some think, posed for it.
